patient.chief_complaint: Prolonged unresponsiveness with eye deviation, stiff posturing — initially diagnosed as stroke, now EEG shows GPDs, team unsure if NCSE
patient.history_present_illness: A 44-year-old Black female social worker presented to a community hospital with acute left gaze deviation, left-sided facial droop, and right-sided arm posturing. Initial NIHSS was 14. The stroke team activated and CT showed no hemorrhage, CTA showed left MCA M1 occlusion. tPA was administered and thrombectomy team was called. During the window for tPA administration, the neurology fellow noted the patient had a brief 30-second rhythmic jerking episode of the right arm that was attributed to post-ischemic cortical spreading depression. NIHSS decreased to 8 after tPA. The patient was transferred to your tertiary center for thrombectomy. On arrival, she is confused, continues with subtle right arm posturing, and has a left gaze preference. EEG was ordered because the floor team was concerned about whether right arm movements were seizure activity. An electroencephalographer notes the EEG shows 'generalized periodic discharges — could be post-tPA ischemic NCSE or metabolic changes.' The team is debating whether to treat as NCSE with benzodiazepines vs proceeding directly with thrombectomy. CRITICAL TIMING ISSUE: Every minute of continued MCA occlusion kills additional brain — thrombectomy must not be delayed, but NCSE could worsen neurological injury if untreated.

family_history: Mother: hypertension, stroke at 62. Father: diabetes. No family history of epilepsy.

neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 12 (E3V3M6). Confused, not following complex commands. Opens eyes to voice. Oriented to name only.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Left gaze deviation (conjugate gaze preference to left). Left facial droop, lower > upper. Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, equal and reactive. Blink reflex intact.
neurological_exam.motor: Right arm posturing (flexor) semi-rhythmically every 30-60 seconds. Left arm moves spontaneously. Right leg weaker than left on cursory exam. Post-tPA NIHSS 8.
neurological_exam.sensory: Unable to assess reliably due to altered consciousness.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Right upper and lower extremity hyperreflexia consistent with acute left hemispheric lesion. Right plantar extensor, left flexor.
neurological_exam.coordination: Not assessable due to confusion and right arm posturing.
neurological_exam.additional: Acute left MCA LVO post-tPA transfer. IIC/LPD pattern on EEG. Thrombectomy takes absolute priority — do NOT delay for EEG evaluation.

findings.morphology: Sharp-wave morphology, periodic with occasional superimposed fast activity — ictal-interictal continuum (IIC) pattern

eeg.impression: This is an ABNORMAL EEG. 1. Lateralized periodic discharges (LPDs) — left hemisphere, maximal at F3, C3, T3; frequency 1.5–2 Hz; sharp-wave morphology with occasional superimposed fast activity (ictal-interictal continuum pattern). 2. Continuous left hemisphere delta activity replacing posterior dominant rhythm. This EEG was obtained under time-limited conditions; full characterization was not possible. Clinical correlation recommended.

Areas of milder DWI restriction in the superior and anterior convexity cortex may represent partial ischemic injury. No haemorrhagic transformation identified on susceptibility-weighted imaging. Geographic infarct distribution consistent with left MCA vascular territory. Clinical correlation recommended.

warnings: No pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic interaction between alteplase and levetiracetam. Levetiracetam does not affect fibrinolysis or coagulation. Safe to administer concurrently with or immediately after tPA.

results.title: Seizures and status epilepticus in acute ischemic stroke: epidemiology and EEG characteristics
results.key_finding: Periodic discharges (LPDs, GPDs) are reported in a substantial proportion of large MCA territory ischemic strokes and are categorized as ictal-interictal continuum patterns. Their electrographic features, temporal relationship to stroke onset and reperfusion, and prognostic significance are described in the literature. Antiseizure medication use in this population and its effect on neurological outcomes have been examined in observational studies.

output.summary: Published literature documents the prevalence of ictal-interictal continuum EEG patterns (LPDs, GPDs) in acute ischemic stroke, particularly large MCA territory infarcts. Pharmacological interactions between fibrinolytic agents and antiseizure medications, and post-reperfusion seizure rates following mechanical thrombectomy, have been examined in cohort studies. Evidence on antiseizure medication selection and dosing in this setting is described in current stroke and epilepsy guidelines.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Acute left MCA ischemic stroke with post-ischemic LPDs (ictal-interictal continuum) and post-reperfusion seizures requiring concurrent thrombectomy and levetiracetam loading

differential.key_features: Autoimmune panel negative; acute MCA LVO on CT/CTA is the primary diagnosis; LPDs are post-ischemic, not from independent epileptiform process
CTA confirms left M1 occlusion — true LVO; NIHSS 14 with positive CTA rules out Todd's paralysis; post-tPA NIHSS improvement supports true ischemic stroke treatment response
Hyperdense left M1 on CT, positive CTA — LVO confirmed; not hemiplegic migraine

optimal_actions.action: IMMEDIATE thrombectomy — left MCA M1 LVO with ASPECTS 7, within time window; do NOT delay for EEG evaluation
IV levetiracetam 1500 mg loading dose CONCURRENTLY with thrombectomy prep — safe, no interaction with tPA or thrombectomy
Do NOT give IV benzodiazepines for EEG LPDs in acute stroke — lowers BP, worsens cerebral perfusion in penumbra
EEG monitoring 20 minutes pre-procedure to document LPD pattern

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Early post-reperfusion seizures controlled with levetiracetam

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Glucose controlled to 140-180 range during acute ischemia

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Core infarct 40 mL with penumbral salvage

critical_actions: Thrombectomy IMMEDIATELY — do NOT delay for EEG evaluation in acute LVO stroke
IV levetiracetam (not benzodiazepines) for concurrent post-stroke seizure management — benzodiazepines lower BP and worsen penumbral perfusion
Insulin protocol for glucose 192 — hyperglycemia worsens stroke outcomes
Post-thrombectomy cEEG 24 hours for post-reperfusion seizure monitoring
contraindicated_actions: IV benzodiazepines for EEG LPDs in acute stroke — lowers BP, reduces cerebral perfusion pressure in ischemic penumbra
Delaying thrombectomy to evaluate and treat EEG LPDs — every minute of LVO delays costs additional penumbra
Phenytoin for post-stroke seizure prevention — sodium channel blockade worsens ischemic neuronal injury
key_reasoning_points: Acute LVO stroke + EEG changes: thrombectomy takes absolute priority over seizure management — time is brain
LPDs in acute stroke are post-ischemic cortical irritability, not independent NCSE — levetiracetam is appropriate concurrent treatment without delaying thrombectomy
Benzodiazepines in acute stroke: contraindicated as BP-lowering effect reduces cerebral perfusion pressure in ischemic penumbra — levetiracetam is safe
Post-reperfusion seizures are common and expected after LVO recanalization — levetiracetam pre-loading reduces early post-stroke seizure burden
Phenytoin worsens ischemic outcomes via sodium channel blockade and local vasoconstriction — never use phenytoin for post-stroke seizures

red_herrings.data_point: EEG LPDs noted on urgent EEG — read as 'possible NCSE' by resident
red_herrings.intended_effect: Delay thrombectomy while treating presumed NCSE with benzodiazepines
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: LPDs in acute MCA stroke are post-ischemic — do not delay thrombectomy. Treat with levetiracetam concurrently, not benzodiazepines. Thrombectomy is the priority.

red_herrings.data_point: Right arm posturing every 30-60 seconds during EEG recording
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest ongoing motor NCSE requiring immediate benzodiazepine treatment
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Right arm posturing in left MCA stroke is a sign of hemispheric dysfunction (posturing from ischemia + possibly post-ischemic cortical irritability) — NOT sufficient to delay thrombectomy. Levetiracetam loading is appropriate without benzodiazepines.
